subject: Art & Design
title: Photography Ethics: Truth, Consent, and Power
description: A fast breakdown of Photography Ethics: Truth, Consent, and Power for builders.

hook.text: Kevin Carter won a Pulitzer for a photo of a starving child with a vulture. He took his own life months later.

buildup.text: Photography raises ethical questions: when to shoot, when to help, who benefits, and who is exploited.

discovery.text: Consent matters. Photographing vulnerable people without permission can exploit rather than expose injustice.

twist.text: AI can now generate photorealistic images that never happened.

climax.text: The photographer holds power: they choose what to show, what to hide, and how the subject is perceived.

punchline.text: A camera doesn't just capture the world. It shapes how we see it.

quiz.question: Why does photography raise unique ethical questions?
options: The photographer holds power over how subjects are perceived and represented

details.summary: Photography raises ethical questions about truth (manipulation vs. authenticity), consent (photographing people without permission), and power (whose stories are told and by whom).
details.whyItMatters: In an era of deep fakes and image manipulation, photographic ethics matter more than ever. Who photographs whom, how images are used, and what truth they claim to represent are questions every photographer must consider.
takeaways: Photography raises questions about truth and manipulation
Consent and power dynamics affect whose stories get told
The camera is never neutral — framing shapes narrative

faq.question: Is it ethical to edit photographs?
faq.answer: Basic adjustments (exposure, contrast, cropping) are universally accepted. Removing or adding elements crosses into manipulation for documentary and journalistic contexts but is standard in commercial and artistic photography.

faq.question: Should you ask permission before photographing strangers?
faq.answer: Legally, public photography is usually permitted. Ethically, it depends on context. Photographing vulnerable people (homeless individuals, children, disaster victims) without consent raises serious ethical concerns. Many photographers ask when practical and avoid exploitative representations.
